Everything you'll see is commit four six one six F C seven, on Godot four point seven point two.

beats.narration_text: Here's where the hull starts: the character sheet. Yoon-chee Zee is filled solid black at game size, about sixty-four pixels across. The first box model failed: facing up and facing down looked the same. So the student added a wide dozer blade at the front and a narrower storage box at the back. Now the silhouette tells you which way the tank faces, before any texture exists.

beats.narration_text: The generation was image to image: Stable Diffusion XL starts from a guide picture. The first guide was flat boxes with black outlines. At denoise point five five, the output was the guide again. At point seven, still flat. At point eight, panel lines finally appear, and the dozer blade is gone. The student kept the seed and prompt fixed and changed one number, so the three are comparable.

beats.narration_text: The diagnosis: flat colors with outlines read as a flat drawing, so the model drew a flat drawing. Claude rewrote the guide in code. This function gives every face its own gradient, a little lighter at the top and a little darker at the bottom. A second script adds grain and grime, with a fixed seed. Same tank, now shaded like an object.

def grad_fill(color, k, pts2d):
    ys=[p[1] for p in pts2d]; y0,y1=min(ys),max(ys)
    if y1-y0<1: y1=y0+1
    gid[0]+=1; i=f"g{gid[0]}"
    c1=D.shade(color,k*1.12); c2=D.shade(color,k*0.82)
    defs.append(f'<linearGradient id="{i}" gradientUnits="userSpaceOnUse" x1="0" y1="{y0:.1f}" x2="0" y2="{y1:.1f}"><stop offset="0" stop-color="{c1}"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="{c2}"/></linearGradient>')
    return f"url(#{i})"

beats.narration_text: And that's the visible result of those lines. On the left, v1: flat fills and hard outlines. On the right, v2: the faces shade from light to dark, and there are road wheels, deck panels and blade ribs for the model to follow. It's the same box model underneath, so the proportions from the character sheet survive.

Same seed, same prompt, the v2 guide, denoise point five five. This is the raw output, straight from the model, and these settings are read from the file's own metadata, not from the log. They match the asset log. Worn olive paint, rust, wheels, and the blade survived. At point six five, the model added a turret dome on the hull, so that one was rejected.

beats.narration_text: Here's the check sheet that caught it. Top row: the cutouts, and the right-facing blade is back. Second row: the red outline of the v2 guide over each hull; the log reports an overlap of point nine nine. Then the turret guide on top, and finally sixty-four pixels on mud, with the silhouette beside it. The facing still reads.

Then colour. The down hull came out about fifteen to twenty percent brighter than the right one. This function measures each sprite's average olive, computes one gain per colour channel toward the sheet's main paint colour, and applies it only where a pixel is olive. Steel, tracks and barrel keep their own colour.

props.title: Colour Match to the Sheet

cues.label: blended in only on olive pixels

props.code:
def color_match(path):
    im=np.asarray(Image.open(path).convert("RGBA")).copy()
    rgb=im[...,:3].astype(np.float32); before=olive_mean(im)
    gain=np.clip(TARGET/np.maximum(before,1),0.75,1.3)
    w=olive_weight(rgb)[...,None]
    rgb=rgb*(1-w)+np.clip(rgb*gain,0,255)*w
    im[...,:3]=np.clip(rgb,0,255).astype(np.uint8)
    Image.fromarray(im,"RGBA").save(path)

beats.narration_text: The result: hull and turret in all eight facings. Five were generated; down-left, left and up-left are mirrors. The olive now matches across directions, and the white stripe, painted on by a script, reads in every one. The log is honest about the leftovers: the up and right turrets have no commander cupola, a one-to-two pixel difference at game size.

Now into the engine. In tank dot G D, the hull picks one of the eight sprites from the movement direction, and only while you're moving. The turret picks its own from the aim. Line one twenty-eight is the state change: moving gives a fast track rumble, idle gives a slower engine shake a third the size. Those are code, not generated frames.

func _on_player_destroyed(_tank) -> void:
	audio.music_stop()  # failure: the music cuts, only the explosion tail remains
	message.text = "YunqiZ destroyed - respawning"
	message.visible = true
	_update_hud()
	await get_tree().create_timer(2.0).timeout
	if level_won or not player.is_dead:
		return
	player.reset_full(SPAWN)
	message.visible = false
	audio.music_start()  # respawn: the music restarts from the beginning
	_update_hud()

props.code:
## level_won is checked and set before the victory sound, so the sound can only play once.
func _on_enemy_destroyed(_tank) -> void:
	remaining = maxi(0, remaining - 1)
	_update_hud()
	if remaining == 0 and not level_won:
		level_won = true
		player.controls_enabled = false
		audio.music_stop()
		audio.play("victory")
		_show_victory()

beats.narration_text: I ran it on an isolated copy of this commit. Eight of eight pass, exit code zero. But look at the last lines. The test report says the leak warnings were fixed by freeing the scene. They still print: twenty-two leaked objects, and seven resources still in use. That doesn't fail the test, but the report's claim doesn't match this run.

props.title: Result: The Recorded Test Run
props.status: RECORDED OUTPUT · run by Claude on an isolated copy, 2026-10-06

beats.narration_text: What that test can't prove: it counts requests to play a sound, not sound reaching your ears, and it skips physics timing by calling handlers directly. The rest was checked by a person. The student played with sound on, then muted, like this screenshot, and listened for the loop seam. Nobody else has played it yet, and the low cannon and explosion were never checked on laptop speakers.

Which model made which asset. Stable Diffusion XL Base one point oh, running locally in ComfyUI, made the hull and turret sprites, the three cover stages, and the ground. Stable Audio three Small, the S F X version, made the cannon, the cover hit, the tank hit and the explosion. The music version made the victory sting and the battle loop. The flashes, smoke, fire and explosions you saw are code particles, not model output.

props.title: Which Model Made Which Asset
props.status: FROM ASSET-LOG.md AND SOURCES.md · the real files

beats.narration_text: Who did what. The student chose the game, the pillars, the blade and the box, ran every generation, and judged every output. Claude drew the guides in code, drafted the prompts, and wrote the cleanup scripts and all the game code. The models made pixels and waveforms. One example from the log: the student first preferred denoise point seven five. Claude pointed out that the stripe was gone and the shape had drifted. The student chose point six.

What's still uncertain. The logs disagree about the kept down turret: the asset log says denoise point six, with an unrecorded seed. The file itself says point five five and gives the seed, which matches the Frictional log. The environment generations have no asset log rows, a few referenced check images aren't in this commit, and the fresh-copy run is still marked to do. Next step toward the full game: give the enemy tanks their own generated design, instead of a grey tint.

props.title: Still Uncertain, and the Next Step

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Observed in a scripted run, not a human playtest: all eight facings, idle and moving, firing, cover cracking and breaking, smoke, flames, destruction, respawn, pause and victory, with all five sound events. The music cut on each death, restarted on respawn, held its place on pause, and stopped at victory. The test passes eight of eight, with leak warnings the report says are gone. Not shown: the mute keys and restart. Untested: other players and laptop speakers. And the logs need a pass.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt. Please use Walker to add one new sound event to my walker-TANK slice: a short click when the zero point eight second reload finishes. First add it to my event-to-sound map, and predict how many clicks ten seconds of held fire should give. Then extend tests slash test sound triggers to count it, and only then edit the game code. That prompt puts the prediction and the test before the code, the same order this slice used for its other five sounds. When the answer comes back, compare its number with yours before you listen. Then play it, sound on and muted. Liam, in for Bear.
